analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers for their emissions and pays the money back as monthly dividends to Americans.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 86 cosponsors, including one Republican, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died when Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge oil refineries, coal mines, and natural gas pipelines a fee for the greenhouse gases their fuels produce, starting at $15 per ton and rising $10 each year. The money would go into a trust fund and be paid out as equal monthly dividends — one full share per adult, half per child — to nearly every American citizen and lawful resident. To avoid double regulation, it would pause certain EPA greenhouse gas rules, with the rules automatically restored if emissions targets were missed, and it would place fees on imports from countries without comparable carbon prices so U.S. manufacturers are not undercut.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly every U.S. citizen and lawful resident would receive a monthly dividend check; because each adult gets the same share while wealthier households buy far more fuel, most low- and middle-income households would come out ahead financially even after paying higher energy prices. People on federal or state assistance would benefit twice, since the dividend could not be counted as income or resources against their benefits. Cleaner air from reduced fossil fuel use would help everyone, and carbon-intensive U.S. manufacturers would gain protection against imports from countries with no carbon price.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Most American households, especially lower-income ones

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund that pays every eligible adult one full pro-rata share and each child half a share every month, funded entirely by the carbon fee.

Because the fee is charged upstream (refineries, coal mines, gas pipelines) but the dividend is equal per person, households that use less energy than average — typically lower-income households — would receive more in dividends than they pay in higher fuel prices.
The dividend is excluded from income and resource calculations for any federal, state, or federally funded assistance program, so safety-net recipients would not lose benefits for receiving it.

Sets an escalating fee ($15 per ton in 2019, plus $10 more each year, with automatic increases if emissions targets are missed) aimed at cutting covered-fuel emissions to 10% of 2016 levels over decades, with EPA greenhouse gas rules automatically reinstated if the targets are not met.

Uses a border fee adjustment — fees on carbon-intensive imports like steel, aluminum, cement, and chemicals, with refunds for U.S. exporters — so foreign manufacturers without carbon costs cannot undercut American producers.
Includes practical carve-outs: fuel used on farms and by the Armed Forces gets full refunds of the fee, and facilities that capture and permanently store carbon dioxide get payments back.
Explicitly preserves state climate laws and EPA authority over vehicle standards, so the fee adds to — rather than replaces — most existing climate regulation, and no state law is preempted.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refineries, coal mining operations, natural gas pipeline operators, and importers of those fuels pay the fee directly, and they would pass most of it through to consumers in the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. The burden would fall hardest on the coal industry and on households that burn a lot of fuel — rural drivers, coal-dependent regions, and energy-intensive manufacturers. People in U.S. territories and non-citizens without valid work authorization would pay fuel-price increases without receiving dividends.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise prices for gasoline, heating oil, natural gas, and electricity for every household and business; households that drive long distances or live in coal-dependent regions could pay more in higher energy costs than they receive in dividends, at least while the fee ramps up.
Dividend payments are taxable income, so the net benefit to lower-income households would be somewhat smaller than the gross check.

The bill suspends EPA enforcement of greenhouse gas rules on fuels while the fee is in effect; the backstop only triggers with a determination in 2030, regulations finalized up to two years later, and full make-up reductions allowed up to eight years after that — so if the fee underperformed, regulatory protection would lapse for years.

Coal miners and workers in fossil-fuel-dependent communities would face accelerating job losses as their fuel becomes the most expensive per unit of energy, and the bill contains no dedicated transition assistance for them beyond the general dividend.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is strong for ordinary households: an equal per-person dividend financed by an upstream fee means most people below average energy use would net gain, the money is not counted against benefits, state laws are preserved, and a regulatory backstop restores EPA rules if emissions targets are missed. The real costs are transitional and regional — higher energy prices concentrated on heavy fuel users and coal communities — and the decade-long gap before the regulatory backstop engages is a genuine weakness. On balance, the benefits to most households and the emissions reductions outweigh the drawbacks, though the coal-country pain is real and largely unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees for two years without ever getting a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Deutch introduced the bill on January 24, 2019, joined by six original cosponsors including Republican Rep. Francis Rooney of Florida and Democrat Rep. Dan Lipinski of Illinois.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to three committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs — and the next day it was sent to the Energy subcommittee; no further action was ever taken.
Over the following two years, none of the three committees held a markup or scheduled the bill, and it never reached the House floor; it died on January 3, 2021, when the 116th Congress ended.
Support grew to 86 cosponsors — 85 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans — but the bill's jurisdiction over tax and energy policy put it in committees that never acted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers — especially coal, oil, and natural gas companies — came out ahead: a carbon fee that would have grown by $10 a ton each year was never enacted, and existing EPA greenhouse gas regulation stayed exactly as it was.

for.name: Rep. Ted Deutch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited an original bipartisan group of six cosponsors, including one Republican.

for.name: 85 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the most-cosponsored carbon pricing bills of the Congress.

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor, the sole Republican supporting the bill in the entire House.

for.name: Citizens' Climate Lobby
for.what_they_did: Championed the carbon-fee-and-dividend design and promoted the bill among members of both parties.

against.name: Committee chairs (Richard Neal, Frank Pallone, Eliot Engel)
against.role: Chairs of House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in either of their full committees or the Energy subcommittee, leaving it to die without a vote.

against.name: 196 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill, leaving it with a single Republican supporter and no path to floor action.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed carbon fee legislation that would tax coal, oil, and natural gas production.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 85 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored versus 1 of 197 Republicans — though the sponsor's office billed it as bipartisan and no committee or floor vote ever split by party.

industries.note: Coal has the highest greenhouse gas content per unit of energy, so the escalating fee would hit it hardest and accelerate its decline; the industry's interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the dividends and cleaner air the public would get.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and natural gas producers
industries.note: Refineries and pipeline operators would pay the fee on every ton of carbon in their fuels and pass it to consumers; avoiding the bill kept a rising $10-per-year charge off their products indefinitely.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, chemicals, glass, paper)
industries.note: These industries would pay carbon costs embedded in higher fuel prices, but the bill's border adjustment would fee carbon-intensive imports and refund fees on their exports, shielding them from foreign competitors with no carbon price.

industries.industry: Fluorinated gas manufacturers and industrial users
industries.note: A separate fee at 10% of the carbon fee rate would be imposed on reportable fluorinated greenhouse gases like HFCs and SF6, adding a new cost for refrigeration, electronics, and electrical equipment industries.
A rising price on fossil fuels would make wind, solar, and efficiency investments relatively cheaper, which is the market shift the bill's own findings say it intends to create.
Farm fuel purchases would be fully refunded and non-fossil farm emissions would be exempt, so farmers would get the dividend like everyone else while escaping most of the fee.
